name: Highway Border
description: Flat strip along highway frontage. Young red cedars, pine, and black cherry present. European turf and weeds dominate ground layer. Road edge stress limits some species.
goals: Establish native wildflower and grass buffer. Suppress turf creep from road edge. Reduce mowing frequency over time. Cedars and black cherry are native — protect.
notes: Check local mowing ordinances before reducing mow frequency — highway ROW may be county-maintained. Flat terrain; red cedars and black cherry are native keystone trees. Road edge stress.
known_plantings_2016: Northern Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) — native to SE Iowa riparian zones; planted by Abundant Biology 2016
Shrub Mix — Arrowwood Viburnum, Elderberry, Nannyberry, Serviceberry, Hazelnut

name: Berm Woodland
priority_action: URGENT: Remove all white mulberry. Cut and immediately treat stumps with concentrated glyphosate. Repeat every 6 weeks through growing season.
description: Raised berm landform with mixed woodland. Pine, oak, and black cherry present. White/hybrid mulberry invasion actively being removed. Best woodland edge opportunity on the property. NW corner contains 2020 DNR Songbird Packet planting (White Pine, Bur Oak, Chokecherry, Gray Dogwood, Serviceberry, Wild Plum).
goals: Complete mulberry elimination. Native woodland restoration favoring bur oak, hackberry, and native understory shrubs. Protect and expand from DNR and 2016 plantings.
notes: Mulberry spreads aggressively via bird droppings — remove all fruiting trees first. Scout garlic mustard in spring before seed set. NW corner has 2020 DNR Songbird Packet plantings — protect those seedlings.
known_plantings_2016: Northern Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) — native to SE Iowa; planted by Abundant Biology 2016 (south berm area)
Oak Mix (Pin, White, Red, Bur Oaks)
Arrowwood Viburnum, Elderberry, Nannyberry — Shrub Mix

Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) — DNR Songbird Packet

name: Plateau / Fire Pit
description: First-level plateau area with fire pit. Maple, willows, and birch present. European turf throughout. Good candidate for no-mow native conversion. Consider prairie edge on sunny exposures, woodland floor natives in shade.
goals: Convert turf to native understory. Prairie edge on sunny sides, woodland floor natives in shade. Low maintenance once established.
notes: Keep fire pit area clear 10-foot radius. Good location for fall seeding. Fire-adapted prairie edge on sunny exposures; woodland floor species in shade under existing maples.

name: Home / Drive / Pool
priority_action: Remove Bradford pear entirely — it is invasive and spreads aggressively from seed. Replace with native serviceberry or redbud.
description: Contains 1681 and 1679 houses, garage, drive, pool, car park, and G-Island. Willow, arborvitae, Bradford pear, pine present. Yews as shrubs. European turf throughout plus perennial plot and fenced vegetable garden inside fence.
goals: Remove Bradford pear. Expand native perennial beds. Gradually replace turf with native groundcovers. Maintain vegetable garden inside fence.
invasives: Bradford Pear (Pyrus calleryana) — MUST REMOVE; highly invasive, spreads aggressively from seed
notes: Blue spruce trees present — monitor for Rhizosphaera needle cast; treat with Daconil when new growth reaches 1–2 inches. Norway/Scotch pines — treat annually for Zimmerman pine moth (Bayer Systemic at base). Bradford pear must be fully removed before it spreads further via birds. Fenced vegetable garden separate from restoration goals.

name: Creekside
priority_action: #1 PRIORITY: Cut ALL bush honeysuckle and paint stumps with concentrated glyphosate every 6 weeks through the growing season. It regrows vigorously — do not skip cycles.
description: Creek corridor sloping west to east. Red cedar, river birch, willow, and young bur oak in NW corner. Bush honeysuckle is the #1 threat. Wild sunflowers present. Wet-tolerant species zone with creek hydrology.
goals: Eliminate bush honeysuckle entirely. Establish wet-tolerant native riparian corridor. Protect and nurture the young bur oak in NW corner — flag it so it isn't accidentally mowed.
notes: Young bur oak in NW corner — FLAG IT and protect from deer browse. Honeysuckle leafs out 2–3 weeks BEFORE native plants in spring — easiest to spot and treat then. Creek hydrology supports wet-tolerant species. Re-treat honeysuckle regrowth every 6 weeks all season.

name: Island
description: Small ornamental island. Arborvitaes, choke cherry, blue spruce. Lilacs, hydrangeas, hosta. Purple coneflower, possibly yarrow. Choke cherry is a native keystone species.
goals: Maintain existing plantings. Prune lilacs heavily every year or they spread out of control. Add native wildflowers to understory. Monitor blue spruce for disease.
notes: Prune lilacs heavily — spring immediately after bloom through early summer; NEVER in September (breaks dormancy). Blue spruce treated historically for Rhizosphaera needle cast with Daconil — repeat when new growth is 1–2 inches. Choke cherry is native keystone — protect. Hydrangeas and hosta are non-native ornamentals — acceptable here.

name: NE Native Seed Plot
priority_action: Mow/clear edges to 4–6 inches to suppress turf and brome grass. Hand-weed around seedlings. Kill surrounding turf with glyphosate before fall re-seed if needed.
description: Dedicated prairie establishment plot in NE corner. Hoksey 20-20 prairie mix seeded 2020/2021 — poor results due to turf competition and prep issues. Earth Science native mix seeded May 2024. Establishment is a multi-year project requiring persistent turf suppression.
goals: Establish self-sustaining native prairie. Suppress turf competition — this is the main barrier. Re-seed with Hoksey native mix fall 2025 after full turf kill. Seeds need cold stratification over winter.
notes: Native prairie seedlings look like weeds in years 1–2 — most energy goes to roots. Be very cautious before pulling anything. Mowing to 4–6 inches in summer suppresses weeds without harming prairie plants. Do NOT use herbicide near seedlings. Fall seeding is ideal — cold stratification over winter improves germination.

name: Perennial Plot
description: Very small perennial test bed. Currently planted with Burpee Perennial Wildflower Mix — mostly non-native species (baby's breath, blue flax, lupine, calendula, Siberian wallflower) with some natives mixed in (lanceleaf coreopsis, coneflower, Indian blanket, black-eyed Susan, Mexican hat).
goals: Allow natives to self-seed and expand. Let non-natives fade out naturally over time. Good test bed for trialing species before planting larger areas.
notes: Small enough to maintain entirely by hand. Divide overcrowded perennials in spring or fall. Deadhead through summer to extend bloom; leave seedheads in fall for birds. Supplement with native seed from Hoksey or Prairie Moon Nursery to shift the balance toward Iowa natives.
